Disease
 
Name:
 
Atrial
 
Fibrillation
 
(A-fib)
 
Details:
 
Definition:
 
Atrial
 
fibrillation
 
is
 
a
 
common
 
type
 
of
 
arrhythmia,
 
or
 
irregular
 
heartbeat.
 
In
 
A-fib,
 
the
 
upper
 
chambers
 
of
 
the
 
heart
 
(the
 
atria)
 
beat
 
chaotically
 
and
 
irregularly,
 
out
 
of
 
sync
 
with
 
the
 
lower
 
chambers
 
(the
 
ventricles).
 
This
 
disorganized
 
electrical
 
activity
 
leads
 
to
 
a
 
rapid
 
and
 
irregular
 
heart
 
rhythm.
  
 
How
 
it
 
Works:
 
Normally,
 
the
 
heart's
 
natural
 
pacemaker,
 
the
 
sinoatrial
 
(SA)
 
node
 
located
 
in
 
the
 
right
 
atrium,
 
sends
 
out
 
regular
 
electrical
 
signals
 
that
 
coordinate
 
the
 
contraction
 
of
 
the
 
heart
 
chambers.
 
In
 
A-fib,
 
multiple
 
rapid
 
and
 
disorganized
 
electrical
 
signals
 
fire
 
from
 
different
 
areas
 
in
 
the
 
atria.
 
These
 
chaotic
 
signals
 
overwhelm
 
the
 
SA
 
node,
 
causing
 
the
 
atria
 
to
 
quiver
 
or
 
fibrill
 
instead
 
of
 
contracting
 
effectively.
 
As
 
a
 
result,
 
the
 
atria
 
don't
 
pump
 
blood
 
efficiently
 
into
 
the
 
ventricles.
 
The
 
ventricles
 
then
 
beat
 
irregularly
 
as
 
they
 
respond
 
to
 
the
 
erratic
 
signals
 
from
 
the
 
atria.
 
Causes
 
and
 
Risk
 
Factors:
 
A-fib
 
can
 
be
 
caused
 
by
 
or
 
associated
 
with
 
various
 
factors,
 
including:
 
●
 
Heart
 
conditions:
 
○
 
High
 
blood
 
pressure
 
(hypertension)
 
○
 
Coronary
 
artery
 
disease
 
○
 
Heart
 
failure
 
○
 
Valvular
 
heart
 
disease
 
(e.g.,
 
mitral
 
stenosis,
 
mitral
 
regurgitation)
 
○
 
Pericarditis
 
○
 
Congenital
 
heart
 
defects
 
○
 
Previous
 
heart
 
surgery
 
●
 
Other
 
medical
 
conditions:
 
○
 
Thyroid
 
problems
 
(especially
 
hyperthyroidism)
 
○
 
Chronic
 
lung
 
disease
 
(e.g.,
 
COPD,
 
pulmonary
 
embolism)
 
○
 
Diabetes
 
○
 
Obesity
 
○
 
Sleep
 
apnea
 
○
 
Chronic
 
kidney
 
disease
 
●
 
Lifestyle
 
factors:
 
○
 
Excessive
 
alcohol
 
consumption
 
("holiday
 
heart
 
syndrome")
 
○
 
Stimulants
 
(e.g.,
 
caffeine,
 
certain
 
medications)
 
○
 
Stress
 
●
 
Age:
 
The
 
risk
 
of
 
A-fib
 
increases
 
with
 
age.
 
●
 
Genetics:
 
Some
 
people
 
may
 
have
 
a
 
genetic
 
predisposition
 
to
 
developing
 
A-fib.
 
●
 
Sometimes,
 
the
 
cause
 
of
 
A-fib
 
is
 
unknown
 
(idiopathic).
 
Symptoms:
 
Symptoms
 
of
 
A-fib
 
can
 
vary
 
widely
 
from
 
person
 
to
 
person.
 
Some
 
individuals
 
may
 
experience
 
no
 
symptoms
 
at
 
all,
 
while
 
others
 
have
 
noticeable
 
and
 
bothersome
 
symptoms.
 
Common
 
symptoms
 
include:
 
●
 
Palpitations:
 
A
 
fluttering,
 
racing,
 
pounding,
 
or
 
skipping
 
sensation
 
in
 
the
 
chest.
 
●
 
Shortness
 
of
 
breath
 
(dyspnea):
 
Especially
 
during
 
exertion.
 
●
 
Fatigue
 
and
 
weakness:
 
Feeling
 
unusually
 
tired.
 
●
 
Dizziness
 
or
 
lightheadedness:
 
A
 
feeling
 
of
 
being
 
unsteady
 
or
 
faint.
 
●
 
Chest
 
pain
 
or
 
discomfort:
 
Although
 
less
 
common
 
than
 
in
 
other
 
heart
 
conditions.
 
●
 
Reduced
 
exercise
 
tolerance:
 
Difficulty
 
performing
 
physical
 
activities.
 
Complications:
 
A-fib
 
can
 
lead
 
to
 
significant
 
complications:
 
●
 
Stroke:
 
This
 
is
 
the
 
most
 
serious
 
risk.
 
The
 
irregular
 
beating
 
of
 
the
 
atria
 
can
 
cause
 
blood
 
to
 
pool
 
and
 
form
 
clots.
 
If
 
a
 
clot
 
travels
 
from
 
the
 
heart
 
to
 
the
 
brain,
 
it
 
can
 
block
 
blood
 
flow
 
and
 
cause
 
a
 
stroke.
 
Individuals
 
with
 
A-fib
 
have
 
a
 
significantly
 
increased
 
risk
 
of
 
stroke.
 
●
 
Heart
 
failure:
 
Over
 
time,
 
the
 
rapid
 
and
 
irregular
 
heart
 
rhythm
 
can
 
weaken
 
the
 
heart
 
muscle,
 
leading
 
to
 
heart
 
failure.
 
●
 
Blood
 
clots
 
in
 
other
 
organs:
 
Although
 
less
 
common
 
than
 
stroke,
 
blood
 
clots
 
can
 
travel
 
to
 
other
 
parts
 
of
 
the
 
body.
 
●
 
Reduced
 
quality
 
of
 
life:
 
Symptoms
 
like
 
fatigue
 
and
 
shortness
 
of
 
breath
 
can
 
significantly
 
impact
 
daily
 
activities.
 
Diagnosis:
 
Diagnosis
 
of
 
A-fib
 
typically
 
involves:
 
●
 
Electrocardiogram
 
(ECG
 
or
 
EKG):
 
This
 
is
 
the
 
primary
 
diagnostic
 
tool.
 
It
 
records
 
the
 
electrical
 
activity
 
of
 
the
 
heart
 
and
 
can
 
clearly
 
show
 
the
 
irregular
 
rhythm
 
of
 
A-fib.
 
●
 
Holter
 
monitor:
 
A
 
portable
 
ECG
 
device
 
worn
 
for
 
24-48
 
hours
 
(or
 
longer)
 
to
 
continuously
 
record
 
the
 
heart's
 
rhythm,
 
especially
 
if
 
A-fib
 
episodes
 
are
 
infrequent.
 
●
 
Event
 
monitor:
 
A
 
device
 
worn
 
for
 
several
 
weeks
 
that
 
the
 
patient
 
activates
 
when
 
they
 
feel
 
symptoms.
 
●
 
Echocardiogram:
 
An
 
ultrasound
 
of
 
the
 
heart
 
to
 
assess
 
its
 
structure
 
and
 
function
 
and
 
look
 
for
 
underlying
 
heart
 
conditions.
 
●
 
Blood
 
tests:
 
To
 
check
 
for
 
thyroid
 
problems,
 
electrolyte
 
imbalances,
 
and
 
other
 
conditions
 
that
 
might
 
contribute
 
to
 
A-fib.
 
●
 
Sometimes,
 
more
 
invasive
 
tests
 
like
 
electrophysiological
 
studies
 
(EPS)
 
may
 
be
 
needed.
